1303.title: Adab with children
1303.hook: a kiss for a grandson, a man who never kissed his own, and one short sentence about mercy
1303.howItsDone: The hadith collections show the Prophet kissing his grandson and carrying his granddaughter Umamah in prayer as open tenderness toward children, summed up in the hadith that whoever does not show mercy is not shown mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday: adab with neighbors, safe beside you first, then a little more water in the soup. Today, the smallest people in the house; day two hundred seventy-one let them climb on the Prophet in prayer.

A grandfather bends down and kisses a small boy. Nothing unusual, except who's watching. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, kissed his grandson al-Hasan, while a man named al-Aqra' ibn Habis sat nearby. Al-Aqra' said: I have ten children, and I have never kissed a single one of them. The Prophet looked at him, and his answer was short enough to fit on a fridge.
screen: `A KISS FOR AL-HASAN.` → `TEN CHILDREN, NEVER KISSED.` → `THE PROPHET LOOKED AT HIM.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in paraphrase from Bukhari: whoever does not show mercy is not shown mercy. In Arabic it's short: man la yarham la yurham. One verb, turned from giving mercy to receiving it. He didn't argue about customs or toughness. He tied the kiss to mercy, and mercy to the One who shows mercy. Bukhari keeps a second report like it. A desert Arab came and said, in paraphrase: you kiss children? We don't kiss them. And the Prophet answered: what can I do for you, if Allah has taken mercy from your heart? The problem isn't in the hands. It's in the heart. Then a scene you can see, also in Bukhari, in paraphrase: the Prophet prayed carrying his granddaughter Umamah. When he went down into prostration, he set her down. When he stood, he picked her up again. Nobody sent her out of the room. So adab with children isn't a list of rules for children. It's the adults' manners toward them: tenderness shown openly, affection that doesn't wait for a child to earn it, room for them even in the middle of worship. And the mercy you give a small person is tied, in this hadith, to the mercy you hope to receive.
screen: `WHOEVER SHOWS NO MERCY IS SHOWN NONE.` · `NOT IN THE HANDS. IN THE HEART.` · `UMAMAH CARRIED THROUGH PRAYER.` · `MERCY GIVEN, MERCY RECEIVED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a child in your life, your own, a niece or nephew, a grandchild, a student, and see their face. If one is near you today, the practice is simple: a hug or a kiss on the head, offered openly, with nothing asked back; if not, remember an adult who was gentle with you when you were small. If you pray, you can ask mercy for that child.
Adab with children. The manners of the grown-ups toward the small ones: open tenderness, room for them even in prayer, and mercy given so mercy is received. Today's word.
Your line: mercy for mercy. Given to the small ones, and given back to you. See you tomorrow.

1304.title: Adab with creation
1304.hook: a cat shut in and left hungry, a dog at a well, and a leather sock full of water
1304.howItsDone: Islamic teaching on animals draws on Qur'an 6:38, which calls animals and birds peoples like us, and on hadith such as the woman and the cat and the man who gave water to a thirsty dog.

segments.voice: Yesterday: adab with children, mercy given so mercy is received. Day two hundred seventy-two told today's two stories; today they become a mirror.

A cat, shut in. No food set down, and no way out to hunt for its own. That's the whole story, as Sahih al-Bukhari tells it, in paraphrase: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said a woman entered the Fire because of a cat. She neither fed it nor let it loose to eat the small creatures of the earth. No crime against a person. No grand sin anyone would whisper about. One animal, in her power, and ignored.
screen: `A CAT, SHUT IN.` → `NOT FED. NOT FREED.` → `ONE ANIMAL, IN HER POWER.`

segments.voice: Start with the Qur'an's view of animals. Surah al-An'am, in Pickthall's translation: "There is not an animal in the earth, nor a flying creature flying on two wings, but they are peoples like unto you." Peoples: communities with their own lives, not furniture in ours. Now put the cat beside a second story, also in Bukhari, in paraphrase. A man walking along a road grew desperately thirsty. He found a well, climbed down, and drank. Climbing out, he saw a dog panting, licking damp earth from thirst. He thought: this dog is suffering what I just suffered. So he went back down, filled his leather sock with water, held it in his teeth to climb, and gave the dog a drink. And the Prophet said Allah thanked him for it, and forgave him. The companions were surprised. They asked: is there reward for us even in animals? His answer, in paraphrase: in every living thing with a moist liver, there is reward. A body that is alive; that's the whole qualification. The two stories mirror each other. One person had an animal in her control and did nothing. One had no duty to a stray dog at all, and went back down the well. Adab with creation lives in the space between: when something weaker is thirsty in front of you, noticing it, the way the man noticed: this is what I just felt.
screen: `AL-AN'AM: PEOPLES LIKE UNTO YOU.` · `A DOG AT THE WELL.` · `A MOIST LIVER, A REWARD.` · `TWO STORIES, ONE MIRROR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the animals that cross your day: a pet asleep on the couch, pigeons at the bus stop, a stray cat under a parked car. Choose one and ask the man's question at the well: what does this creature need that I happen to have, water in a bowl, crumbs where it's allowed, a fresh dish set down with attention? If you pray, you can remember that creature in your prayer.
Adab with creation. The manners owed to every living thing: not leaving it hungry in your power, and going back down the well when it's thirsty. Today's word.
Your line: every creature counts. Anything with a moist liver is in the circle. Tomorrow, adab with the earth.

the rules for which animals may be eaten and which may not

1305.title: Adab with the earth
1305.hook: the end of the world arrives, and there's a seedling in your hand
1305.howItsDone: Islamic teaching on the earth draws on the Qur'an's description of humanity as khalifa, a steward on the earth, and on hadith that count planting as charity and that urge planting a seedling even when the Hour comes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: adab with creation, from the cat shut in to the dog at the well. Today, the ground they all stand on, which day six hundred eighty-four asked us not to spoil.

The Hour has come. The end of everything. And there you are, holding a small palm shoot, roots still in a clump of soil. What now? The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, answered that exact question. In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, in paraphrase: if the Hour is established and one of you has a seedling in his hand, and he is able to plant it before he stands up, let him plant it.
screen: `THE HOUR HAS COME.` → `A SEEDLING IN YOUR HAND.` → `PLANT IT.`

segments.voice: Sit with how strange that is. If the world is ending, nobody will eat the dates or rest in the shade. And still: plant it. The hadith pulls the act loose from its result. Then the Qur'an gives the reason the earth is in our hands at all. Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." Khalifa: a deputy, a steward, someone looking after what belongs to another. In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, the Prophet adds: the world is sweet and green, and Allah has made you successors in it, to see how you act. Stewards are watched for how they treat the estate. Then a hadith that turns the garden into worship. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: whenever a Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop, and a bird, or a person, or an animal eats from it, it counts as charity for him. By that hadith, even the sparrow that steals your figs leaves a charity behind. So the adab with the earth comes down to three movements. Plant, even when you won't see the fruit. Look after it as a steward, not an owner. And let the birds have their share. That closes the manners of daily life, down to the soil underfoot. Tomorrow the path turns inward, to the virtues.
screen: `PLANT IT, EVEN AT THE END.` · `A VICEROY IN THE EARTH.` · `SWEET AND GREEN, AND WATCHED.` · `THE BIRD'S SHARE IS CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Feel your weight resting on the ground, or on a floor built on the ground, and bring to mind one small patch of earth you can reach: a pot on the windowsill, a yard, a crack in the sidewalk where something is already trying. Picture putting something into it, a seed, a cutting, or water for a thirsty plant, and notice you don't need to see it grow. If you pray, you can offer that small planting with the remembrance of Allah.
Adab with the earth. The manners of a steward: planting even when you won't see the fruit, looking after what was entrusted, and letting the birds have their share. Today's word.
Your line: plant it anyway. The birds get their share too. Rest well.

1306.title: Humility that raises
1306.hook: one hadith promises that the way up runs downward
1306.howItsDone: Muslim teaching on tawadu' draws on Qur'an 25:63 and the hadith that no one humbles himself for Allah except that Allah raises him, and on reports of the Prophet serving his family at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday: adab with the earth, plant it anyway, and let the birds have their share. Today the path turns from manners to the virtues underneath them.

Where do you sit when you walk into a crowded room? Near the front, where you'll be seen? By the door, where you can slip out? Or wherever's left? One hadith turns the whole question upside down. In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: no one humbles himself for the sake of Allah, except that Allah raises him. The way up runs downward. Today's word: tawadu', humility.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU SIT?` → `HUMBLED FOR ALLAH, RAISED BY ALLAH.` → `TAWADU'.`

segments.voice: Notice the small phrase in the middle: for the sake of Allah. This isn't putting yourself down to be noticed, or false modesty fishing for a compliment. It's lowering yourself where Allah sees it, and leaving the raising to Him. The hadith doesn't say how or when. Only who does it. The Qur'an draws the same posture as a way of walking. Surah al-Furqan, in Pickthall's translation: "The (faithful) slaves of the Beneficent are they who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace." Humility in the feet, and in the reply when someone is rude. Then why it matters between people. In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, the Prophet said Allah revealed to him: be humble toward one another, so that no one boasts over another, and no one wrongs another. Pride isn't only a private flaw; it's where boasting and wronging start. And in a life? Someone asked 'A'ishah what he did at home. Her answer, in Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: he was in the service of his family, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray. And Anas reports, also in Bukhari, that any slave girl of Medina could take the Prophet by the hand and lead him wherever she needed. So tawadu' isn't a mood of feeling small. It's a set of movements: the lower seat, the soft step, the chores at home, the hand that lets itself be taken.
screen: `FOR THE SAKE OF ALLAH, NOT FOR SHOW.` · `AL-FURQAN: WALKING MODESTLY.` · `NO ONE BOASTS, NO ONE WRONGS.` · `IN THE SERVICE OF HIS FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Picture one place you'll sit today, a meeting, a table, a bus, and in your mind take the lower seat there, letting someone else have the better chair, the first word, the credit. Notice what pulls at you without arguing with it, then see yourself quietly doing one chore you usually leave to someone else. If you pray, you can make that small lowering for the sake of Allah.
Tawadu'. Humility: lowering yourself for the sake of Allah, in your seat, your step and your service, and leaving the raising to Him. Today's word.
Your line: lowered, raised. You do the lowering; the raising is left to Him. See you tomorrow.

1307.title: Generosity that draws near
1307.hook: a saying that measures generosity in distance: near Allah, near people
1307.howItsDone: Muslims give through zakat, sadaqah and everyday hospitality, often recalling the hadith to give without counting and Qur'an 76:9, giving for the sake of Allah without wanting thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tawadu', humility, lowered for Allah and raised by Him. Today, a virtue measured in distance.

Near, and far. That's the whole frame of a saying recorded by al-Tirmidhi. In paraphrase, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: the generous one is near to Allah, near to the Garden, near to people, and far from the Fire. And the miser is far from Allah, far from the Garden, far from people, and near the Fire. Generosity isn't measured here in dollars. It's measured in distance: who you end up close to.
screen: `NEAR, AND FAR.` → `NEAR ALLAH, NEAR PEOPLE.` → `MEASURED IN DISTANCE.`

segments.voice: Start with the people part, because it's the one you can test. Stinginess pushes people off. The friend who passes the dish first is easy to sit beside. The saying claims the same holds with Allah. The Qur'an shows what this giving sounds like from inside. In surah al-Insan, the righteous feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, and say, in Pickthall's translation: "We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you." The gift isn't a loan of gratitude. Then Asma', the daughter of Abu Bakr. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, she came to the Prophet with a question. She had nothing of her own, only what her husband al-Zubayr brought home. Could she give from that? His answer: give, and don't count, or Allah will count against you. Don't hoard, or Allah will withhold from you. That's the edge of this virtue: not a measured amount after checking the balance twice, but a hand a little more open than is comfortable. And Bukhari keeps one more picture, in paraphrase: every morning two angels come down. One says: O Allah, give the one who spends something in its place. The other says: O Allah, bring loss to the one who holds back. In the hadith, the giver isn't emptied; something comes back. So: give for Allah, not for thanks. Give without counting. And, in the saying's own terms, the open hand ends up closer to Allah, and to people.
screen: `STINGINESS PUSHES PEOPLE OFF.` · `AL-INSAN: NO REWARD NOR THANKS.` · `ASMA': GIVE, AND DON'T COUNT.` · `TWO ANGELS EACH MORNING.`

segments.voice: Open your hands on your knees, palms up, and notice how that feels compared to a closed fist. Bring to mind one thing you could give, money, food, time, a compliment you've been holding back, and notice the moment your mind starts counting: is it enough, is it too much? Let the counting go quiet and see yourself handing it over; if you pray, make the intention for the sake of Allah.
Generosity that draws near. Giving for Allah and not for thanks, without counting, so that the giver ends up near Allah and near people. Today's word.
Your line: near through giving. Measured in distance, not in dollars. Tomorrow, a quieter virtue.

1308.title: Modesty brings good
1308.hook: a man scolds his brother for being too shy, and the Prophet steps in
1308.howItsDone: In Islamic teaching, haya', modesty and shyness before people and before Allah, is part of faith, drawing on hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari that say haya' brings nothing but good.

segments.voice: Yesterday: generosity that draws near, giving without counting. Today, a quieter virtue that holds back instead, the one day five hundred twenty-five called a walk.

A man of the Ansar is lecturing his brother: you're too shy. You hold back too much. It's costing you. It's the kind of advice people still give. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was passing by and heard it. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, he said: leave him. Haya' is part of faith. He didn't side with the confident brother. He defended the shy one.
screen: `YOU'RE TOO SHY.` → `LEAVE HIM.` → `HAYA' IS PART OF FAITH.`

segments.voice: Haya' is hard to put into one English word: modesty, shyness, a sense of shame in the good sense, the inner brake that stops a hand before it does something low. The hadith of the day is from 'Imran ibn Husayn, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: haya' brings nothing but good. Not mostly good. Only good. It isn't timidity, the fear that keeps someone from speaking a truth. It's closer to conscience with a blush. Abu Sa'id describes the Prophet himself, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: he was more shy than a young girl behind her curtain, and when he disliked something, you could see it in his face. Then Bukhari keeps a saying the Prophet traced to the words of the first prophecy, in paraphrase: if you have no haya', do whatever you like. It reads like permission, but it's a warning. Without that inner brake, nothing stops anything. Haya' is the pause before the cruel comment, the post that shows off, the glance that takes too much. Tradition speaks of it facing two ways: haya' before people, and haya' before Allah, the sense of being seen even when the room is empty. Both make a person a little slower to do what they'd regret. That's why it brings only good.
screen: `MODESTY, SHYNESS, AN INNER BRAKE.` · `ONLY GOOD, NOT MOSTLY GOOD.` · `NO HAYA'? DO WHAT YOU LIKE.` · `BEFORE PEOPLE, BEFORE ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Run back through yesterday and look for a moment where a small pause might have helped: a joke one step too far, a story told mostly to look good, something shared that didn't need sharing. Don't judge it; just find the spot where the brake could have touched, and choose one place today to let haya' work, speaking a little less about yourself or letting someone's mistake go unmentioned. If you pray, you can ask for haya'.
Haya'. Modesty and shyness, an inner brake before people and before Allah, that the hadith says brings nothing but good. Today's word.
Your line: only good. Not mostly good, but only good. Tomorrow, truthfulness and the company it keeps.

the shame you feel after you've already done wrong

1309.title: Truthfulness and its company
1309.hook: a man with no excuse tells the truth anyway, and a verse comes down about the company he keeps
1309.howItsDone: Islamic teaching draws on Qur'an 9:119 and the story of Ka'b ibn Malik: truthfulness is both a personal virtue and a matter of keeping truthful company.

segments.voice: Yesterday: haya', the inner brake that brings only good. Today, the virtue that refuses to hide behind an excuse, in a story first told on day two hundred eighty-two.

Ka'b ibn Malik had no excuse. The army had marched out to Tabuk, and he had simply stayed home, putting it off day after day until it was too late. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, came back, others lined up with reasons, and he accepted their word. Then it was Ka'b's turn. He could talk well. He knew he could win the moment. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, he told the Prophet instead: I had no excuse.
screen: `STAYED HOME FROM TABUK.` → `OTHERS BROUGHT EXCUSES.` → `KA'B: I HAD NO EXCUSE.`

segments.voice: It cost him. Ka'b, with two others who also told the truth, was set apart. People stopped speaking to them. Ka'b says the earth, wide as it was, felt narrow. Then the Qur'an spoke about the three. Surah al-Tawbah describes them, and their repentance accepted, then turns to everyone listening. In Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Be careful of your duty to Allah, and be with the truthful." Not only be truthful. Be with the truthful. Sidq is a virtue, and it is also a company. And Ka'b, after all of it, said, in paraphrase from Bukhari: Allah saved me only through truthfulness, and part of my repentance is to speak nothing but the truth for the rest of my life. Then the Prophet's own description, from Ibn Mas'ud, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to the Garden, and a person keeps telling the truth until he becomes a siddiq, one utterly truthful. Each true sentence is a step, and the steps add up to a name. That's why the company matters. A circle where everyone shades the story makes the next lie cheaper. A circle of truthful friends makes a sentence like Ka'b's easier to say.
screen: `THE EARTH FELT NARROW.` · `AL-TAWBAH: BE WITH THE TRUTHFUL.` · `STEP BY STEP TO SIDDIQ.` · `THE COMPANY YOU KEEP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you spend the most time with, in person or on a screen, and ask of each, without judging anyone: with this person, is it easier to tell the truth, or harder? Then hold the face of one person who tells you the truth even when it's awkward. If you pray, you can ask to be among the truthful.
Sidq. Truthfulness: in the tongue, in the heart, and in the company you keep, step by step toward becoming a siddiq. Today's word.
Your line: with the truthful. A virtue, and a company to keep. I'll be here tomorrow.
